name: service-layer
intent: Define the application's boundary with a layer of services that publishes the set of available operations and coordinates each operation's transaction and response, so that every client layer shares one implementation instead of duplicating the orchestration around the domain model.
problem: Several clients - user interfaces, integration interfaces, batch jobs, other systems - need the same application operations, and each one ends up re-implementing the orchestration, transaction handling and response sequencing around the domain model; the duplicated logic drifts apart and the transaction boundary lives wherever a caller happened to open one.
context: Enterprise applications in which more than one interface or delivery mechanism invokes the same business operations; operations that span several domain objects, repositories or external systems and must run as one unit; and teams that want one published, testable set of operations (invoked locally or remotely) that clients depend on while the model behind it stays free to change.
benefits: One implementation of each operation's orchestration and transaction: every client layer calls the same boundary instead of repeating the load-decide-store-notify sequence.

A stable published operation set: user interfaces, integration interfaces and batch jobs can change or be added without touching the domain model, and the boundary is the natural home of a remote contract.
Transaction demarcation becomes an explicit, owned responsibility of the application layer rather than an accident of whichever UI or framework happened to open a connection.

Domain objects stay focused on domain logic: application-specific coordination (gateways, notifications, workflow steps) lives in the service, so the model remains reusable across applications and interfaces.
The boundary is one place for cross-cutting policy - authorisation checks, audit, idempotency, retry - instead of a copy per client.
tradeoffs: An extra layer of indirection: operations that merely pass through to a repository still need a service method, boundary types and often a mapping.
Drift towards an anemic domain model: it is easier to keep adding rules in the service than in the model, leaving entities as data bags whose invariants nothing enforces.
Service classes accrete: grouping by subject area eventually produces god services with long dependency lists and methods only loosely related to each other.

Transaction subtleties multiply: proxy self-invocation that is not intercepted, long transactions wrapping remote calls, rollback rules that miss checked or declared exceptions, and nesting semantics that differ per framework.
Testing slides from behaviour to orchestration order: mock-heavy service tests break on refactoring rather than on changed behaviour.
Making the layer remote (or reusing it unchanged as the remote interface) turns method-call-shaped code into chatty network traffic unless coarse operations and a Remote Facade are added.
Two competing transaction owners: if a UI, batch script or framework also opens transactions, ownership becomes ambiguous and partially applied operations appear.

participants.responsibility: The interfaces that invoke the application - user interface, integration interfaces, batch jobs, tests; they depend only on the published operations and know nothing about the model's internals.

One class (or module) per subject area that publishes the available operations, implements each as an operation script or as a thin facade over the Domain Model, owns the transaction boundary and coordinates the response.
The explicit set of operations visible at the boundary - an interface, a remote contract or a module of functions; clients bind to it, not to the implementation classes.
Entities, value objects, aggregates and domain services that hold the domain logic; the service delegates decisions to them and never re-implements them.
The mechanism that begins, commits and rolls back the operation's unit of work - container-managed (EJB, Spring), framework-provided (EF Core, Prisma) or hand-written begin/commit.
The persistence and integration access points the service uses to load and store aggregates and to talk to other systems.
Optional shared base (class or module) that gives every service the same collaborators and common behaviour, so each service does not re-wire the same gateways.

use_cases: An application with more than one client: web UI, public API, admin console, batch job and message consumers all execute the same use cases (place an order, invoice a contract, register a customer).
An operation that must atomically span several aggregates or repositories - reserve stock, create the order, charge the card - with a single commit or rollback.
An integration interface that exposes application operations to partners while keeping the internal model out of the contract, usually together with Remote Facade and Data Transfer Object.
Orchestrating a use case that mixes domain decisions with external systems (payment gateway, e-mail, message broker) so the coordination is written once and can be tested without the UI.
A system that may later add a second delivery channel or move to a workflow engine, where application logic must not be welded to the presentation layer.

Spring Framework applications codify this boundary: service-layer beans are annotated @Transactional and Spring's proxy opens, joins and commits the transaction around each published operation, with rollback rules declared per operation - the framework form of 'the service owns the transaction'.

NestJS applications codify the boundary as providers: @Injectable() service classes hold the business operations and data logic, controllers stay thin and only route HTTP requests to them, and the IoC container injects the services into modules.

Microsoft's tactical DDD guidance for microservices (the eShop reference architectures) prescribes application services that expose use cases by coordinating domain services, aggregates and repositories and manage the transaction, while holding no business rules of their own.
avoid_when: Only one client will ever exist and the logic is thin: transaction scripts called directly from the UI (or plain controller methods) are simpler and honest.
Pure CRUD where each operation is a single repository call: the service layer becomes pass-through indirection - call the repository or active record directly.
A rich domain model with a single in-process client and no cross-cutting transaction or response coordination to add: clients can use the model's own operations.
A throwaway tool, script or prototype with no second consumer of the operations.
The framework already provides the boundary and adding services would only restate it one-to-one per controller method.
anti_patterns: Transaction Script in service clothing: the service contains all the business rules while the entities are passive data structures (the anemic domain model).
God service: one service class per bounded context that accumulates every operation, every dependency and a private helper army.
Pass-through services: one service method per repository method, adding a layer that owns no responsibility.
Layering theatre: services that only rename and forward DAO calls while transactions, validation and orchestration stay in the controllers.
Skipping the boundary for one client, so the same operation enforces different invariants and transactions depending on the entry point.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: application coordination (orchestration, transactions, notifications) is distinct from domain decisions.
Encapsulation of the application boundary: clients depend on a published set of operations, not on the model's internals.
High cohesion, low coupling: one service per subject area, collaborating through explicit interfaces.
Dependency inversion: services depend on abstractions (repositories, gateways) supplied by the composition root.
Information hiding: persistence types, entities and transport shapes do not leak across the boundary.
best_practices: Keep services thin: orchestrate and delegate; put decisions in entities, value objects and domain services.
Own exactly one transaction per operation at the service boundary - not in the UI, not in repositories.
Derive the operation set from the use cases, name operations after business events rather than CRUD calls, and keep the contract stable.
Group operations by subject area and split a service as soon as it needs collaborators from unrelated areas.
Accept and return boundary types (commands, DTOs, results); never expose entities or HTTP/transport concerns across the boundary.
Translate domain errors into application-level outcomes at the boundary and let unexpected exceptions roll the transaction back.
Test orchestration against fake gateways with the real domain objects, and keep rule-focused tests in the domain.
sources: Randy Stafford, 'Service Layer', in Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (Addison-Wesley, 2002), ch. 9 'Domain Logic Patterns', pp. 133-138 - intent, domain facade vs operation script, POJO vs stateless session bean, and the contrast with Session Facade.
